narrative:
The school’s system has analyzed your academic situation and determined that there’s a **24% chance** you might not pass your final year. While this isn’t a certainty, it’s high enough that the school is requiring you to take extra support courses to help you succeed. Think of it like a warning sign—just as you’d pay attention if your car’s check engine light came on, this is the system’s way of saying, *"Let’s address this now before it becomes a bigger issue."*

The decision isn’t random—it’s based on three key factors that stood out in your profile. First, the **reason you chose this school** played a role. Most students who thrive here are focused on the coursework itself, but your primary reason was the school’s reputation. While reputation is great, it can sometimes mean you’re not as deeply engaged with the material as students who are here because they’re passionate about the subject. This isn’t a criticism—it’s just a signal that you might need to connect more personally with your studies to stay on track.

Second, the **support you have at home** is important. You’re lucky to have family who helps you with schoolwork, which many students don’t have. But the system noticed that your family relationships are described as *"good"* rather than *"very good."* Strong family bonds often mean more encouragement, accountability, and resources, which can make a big difference in staying motivated. Even small improvements in this area—like more regular check-ins with your family about your progress—could help you stay focused.

Finally, the **number of past failures** in your classes is a strong indicator. Unlike most students who haven’t struggled before, your record shows no prior failures, which is actually a positive sign. However, the system is flagging that you’re not yet in the top group of students who study the most—you’re spending **2 to 5 hours a week** on coursework, while the highest-performing students study **5 to 10 hours or more**. This isn’t about blaming you; it’s about recognizing that small increases in study time could make a big difference in your confidence and performance.

The good news is that these are all areas you can improve. The remedial courses are designed to give you extra help, but they’ll only work if you use them. Start by setting aside **just 30 minutes more each day** to review material or work on assignments. Talk to your family about how you can make your home environment even more supportive—maybe schedule a weekly study time together or ask older siblings for help. And if you’re not already, try to find one or two subjects you’re genuinely interested in; that curiosity will make studying feel less like a chore.

This isn’t a reflection of your ability—it’s a chance to get ahead. The students who succeed the most aren’t always the ones who start out strongest; they’re the ones who listen to these early signals and adjust. You’ve got this.
